citation.title: Inference in Spatial Experiments with Interference using the SpatialEffect Package
citation.venue: Journal of Agricultural, Biological, and Environmental Statistics

standing_assumptions:
(S1) Setting [Section 2.1, p. 141 (PDF p. 4)]. “Specifically, suppose that we have a set of intervention nodes indexed by $i = 1, ..., N$, and these nodes are arrayed as points in a spatial field, $\mathcal{X}$. Each point in this spatial field, $x \in \mathcal{X}$, equals a coordinate vector of length 2 (recording, e.g., longitude and latitude coordinates). For point interventions, the coordinates of an intervention node $i$ can be given by $x(i)$.” “For each intervention node, we have a binary random variable $Z_i \in \{0, 1\}$ that connotes whether, at node $i$, treatment is activated ($Z_i = 1$) or not ($Z_i = 0$). Denote the ordered vector of random treatment assignments as $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, ..., Z_N)'$, with support $\mathcal{Z}$. We define potential outcomes such that at each point $x \in \mathcal{X}$, we would have outcome $Y_x(\mathbf{z})$ when the treatment assignment is such that $\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}$, and these potential outcomes are defined for each $\mathbf{z} \in \mathcal{Z}$. We stress that outcomes are defined at all $x$ values in $\mathcal{X}$, not just at the $x(i)$ values, which makes the setting bipartite.” “The outcome that we observe at point $x$, labeled $Y_x$, is the potential outcome associated with the realized treatment assignment vector: $Y_x = \sum_{\mathbf{z} \in \mathcal{Z}} Y_x(\mathbf{z})\mathbf{1}(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$, where $\mathbf{1}(\cdot)$ is the indicator function.” “(i.e., we allow for effects to be nonlinear and heterogenous).” Points and polygons [p. 141]: “these intervention nodes could be points or polygons. Wang et al. (2022) show that the analysis is essentially the same, and so for illustration here we will focus on point interventions.”

(S2) Design [Section 2.1, p. 142 (PDF p. 5)]. “Our analysis focuses on randomized experiments for which the distribution of the treatment assignment vector, $\mathbf{Z}$, is known. Our inferential results are derived from the treatment assignment distribution. Extensions to observational studies would follow if the treatment assignment mechanism resembled the kind of Bernoulli process assumed in Wang et al. (2022).” [Section 2.2, p. 142] “$\alpha$ is the experimental design parameter that governs the distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ (that is, the probabilities of different treatment assignment vectors), $\mathbf{z}_{-i}$ is a vector of treatment values at nodes other than node $i$, and $\mathcal{Z}_{-i}$ is the set of possible values that $\mathbf{Z}_{-i}$ can take. The design parameter, $\alpha$, is an abbreviated way of capturing a variety of factors that might affect the distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$. For example, it could index vectors of treatment assignment probabilities for the intervention nodes, where such probabilities would determine the level of treatment saturation. It could also index the correlation structure for the treatments, which would characterize potential restrictions (for example, stratification or clustering) on the profiles of possible treatment assignments.”

(S3) Marginalized outcomes and point effects [Section 2.2, p. 142 (PDF p. 5)]. “we rewrite the potential outcome at point $x$ as $Y_x(Z_i, \mathbf{Z}_{-i})$, where $\mathbf{Z}_{-i}$ is the treatment status of all the intervention nodes except for node $i$. To concentrate on the effect generated by node $i$, we hold node $i$ to treatment value $z$ and marginalize over this variation in $\mathbf{Z}_{-i}$ to define an “individualistic” average of potential outcomes at point $x$: $Y_{ix}(z;\alpha) = \mathrm{E}_{\mathbf{Z}_{-i}}\left[Y_x(z, \mathbf{Z}_{-i})\right] = \sum_{\mathbf{z}_{-i} \in \mathcal{Z}_{-i}} Y_x(z, \mathbf{z}_{-i})\Pr(\mathbf{Z}_{-i} = \mathbf{z}_{-i}; \alpha)$.” “This allows us to define the causal effect at point $x$ of intervening on node $i$, allowing other nodes to vary as they otherwise would under $\alpha$: $\tau_{ix}(\alpha) = Y_{ix}(1;\alpha) - Y_{ix}(0,\alpha)$.” (The comma in the last term is the paper's.)

(S4) Circle averages and the AMR [Section 2.2, p. 143 (PDF p. 6)]. “$\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{z}); d) = \frac{1}{|\{x : d_i(x) = d\}|}\int_{x : d_i(x) = d} Y_x(\mathbf{z})\,\mathrm{d}\zeta$, where $d_i(x) = ||x(i) - x||$ is some well-defined metric that defines whether point $x$ is within a specified distance from intervention node $i$, which is located at $x(i)$, and $\zeta$ is a suitable integration measure.” “$\mu_i(z; d, \alpha) = \mathrm{E}_{\mathbf{Z}_{-i}}[\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}(z, \mathbf{Z}_{-i}); d)]$ is the potential $d$-radius circle average around node $i$, given that node $i$ is assigned to treatment condition $z$ and marginalizing over possible assignments to other points.” “$\tau_i(d; \alpha) = \mu_i(1; d, \alpha) - \mu_i(0; d, \alpha)$, is the average of individualistic responses for points along the circle of radius $d$ around node $i$.” The AMR for distance $d$ is denoted $\tau(d;\alpha)$; its display is misprinted (P008-T14 gives it as printed and corrected): $\tau(d;\alpha) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tau_i(d;\alpha)$.

(S5) Estimator [Section 2.3, pp. 143–144 (PDF pp. 6–7)]. “the preferred estimator for practical purposes is the Hajek estimator (Särndal et al. 1992, pp. 182-184), given by: $\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(d) = \frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i=1}^{N} Z_i\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}; d) - \frac{1}{N_0}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(1 - Z_i)\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}; d)$ where $N_1 = \sum_{i=1}^{N} Z_i$ and $N_0 = N - N_1$.” Here $\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}; d)$ is the circle average of the observed outcomes.

(S6) Hypotheses and the two inference methods [Section 2.3, p. 144 (PDF p. 7)]. “The sharp null hypothesis states that the interventions have no effects whatsoever, such that $Y_x(\mathbf{Z}) = Y_x(\mathbf{0})$ , in which case all unit-level effects are also zero and the AMR is zero. If one assumes that the sharp null hypothesis holds, then the randomization distribution of the AMR can be simulated by simply permuting treatment assignment, estimating the AMR under each of these permutations, and then collecting the resulting set of estimates (Imbens and Rubin 2015, Ch. 5). The resulting distribution is referred to as the null permutation distribution.” The weak null hypothesis is “that the AMR equals zero”. The second method “provides confidence intervals that combine a normal approximation with a nonparametric spatial heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent (spatial-HAC) standard error estimator as proposed by Conley (1999).”

(S7) Package conventions [Section 3, pp. 145–146 (PDF pp. 8–9)]. [p. 145] “Users can choose a set of points that form the edge of a circle of radius $d$, that form a circular band (“donut”) centered at radius $d$, or that form a sector centered at $d$ (“disk”), by altering the option cType. When ras_Z is provided, the distance will be calculated from the boundary of each polygon and we implement polygon intervention. Otherwise, it is calculated from the center of each intervention node and point intervention is implemented.” [p. 145] “For the asymptotic variance estimator, users need to specify a distance threshold (cutoff) beyond which interference dependence does not exist.” [p. 146] “For a specified error rate of $\delta$ (e.g., $\delta = 0.05$), it is the $\delta/2$ and $1-\delta/2$ percentiles of the sharp null distribution generated by permutation. At each distance $d$, the sharp null hypothesis of no effect is rejected if the AMR estimate is smaller than the $\delta/2$ percentile or larger than the $1 - \delta/2$ percentile.” [p. 146] “The SpatialEffectTest() function generates the null permutation distribution of the sum of the AMR estimates within the specified range.”

(S8) Toy example [Sections 4–5, pp. 146–150 (PDF pp. 9–13)]. “The toy example includes 4 intervention nodes in a spatial field where outcomes are recorded in a 4-by-4 raster (left plot of Fig. 2).” “We suppose Bernoulli random assignment of the nodes to treatment, in which case there are 16 ways treatment could be applied, all with equal probability.” [pp. 147–148] “we choose dVec to be a sequence from 0.1 to 2 with an interval length of 0.1. The cutoff point for the spatial HAC variance is set to be 0.4 and the number of permutations is set to be 1000.” Footnote 5 [p. 148]: “The number doesn't make any difference here as there are in total 6 assignments.” (The six assignments are those with two of the four nodes treated, as in the observed assignment.)

(S9) Points the paper leaves open, fixed here so that the targets are definite (these are conventions of this file, not statements of the paper). (i) The paper does not say how a “quantile” or “percentile” of a finite permutation distribution is computed. The staged implementations call R's quantile() with its default rule (type 7): for order statistics $x_{(1)} \le \dots \le x_{(n)}$ and $q \in [0,1]$, with $h = 1 + (n-1)q$, $j = \lfloor h \rfloor$ and $g = h - j$, $Q_7(q) = (1-g)x_{(j)} + g\,x_{(j+1)}$ (and $Q_7(1) = x_{(n)}$). The printed toy percentiles $\mp 7.97$ are reproduced by this rule and lie strictly inside the range of the six enumerated values. (ii) $Y_{ix}(z;\alpha)$ uses $Y_x(z, \mathbf{z}_{-i})$ for every $\mathbf{z}_{-i} \in \mathcal{Z}_{-i}$ and both $z \in \{0,1\}$; a statement below that uses it assumes potential outcomes are defined at each such argument (for instance on all of $\{0,1\}^N$). (iii) $\mathcal{Z}$ is finite, so every expectation over $\mathbf{Z}$ is a finite sum. For a finite set of outcome points with counting measure the circle average is the arithmetic mean over the points with $d_i(x) = d$; every example below is of this kind or has outcomes constant on the circles concerned. (iv) The paper has no numbered results, no appendix and no proofs; every target is an unnumbered statement or display, located by page.

Scope of the list. The paper is a tutorial with no numbered results and no proofs. Three of its eight headline claims contain mathematical statements and enter as headline targets: P008-H1 (the definition of the AMR and its circle-average identities, P008-T25), P008-H2 (the sharp and weak null hypotheses, P008-T26, and the attributed consistency and normality statement, P008-T28) and P008-H6 (the additive case of the attributed equivalence with a structural coefficient, P008-T27). P008-H3, P008-H4 and P008-H5 are a simulated illustration, an empirical estimate and its interpretation; P008-H7 and P008-H8 describe the method and the package. Twelve confirmed errors have corrections that change a mathematical statement, a formula or a constant and are targets: P008-N012 (Major; the reference law of the Uganda permutation test), P008-E002 (Moderate; the percentile rule and the toy example's rejection), P008-N002 (Moderate; the toy example's cutoff), P008-N016 (Moderate; the sum of AMR estimates read as a change in a probability), P008-E015 (Moderate; the bandwidth formula of the archived variance code), P008-E003 (Minor; 12.38 for 8.00), P008-E004 (Minor; the step 5/111 for 0.5/111), P008-E005 (Minor; the misprinted display of the AMR), P008-E007 (Minor; the band described as a set of intervention nodes), P008-N001 (Minor; the band as described and as implemented), P008-N004 (Minor; the scale of the effect function in Figure 2) and P008-N009 (Minor; what the estimate at distance 0 averages). P008-E015, P008-N001, P008-N004 and P008-N009 set a sentence or figure of the article against the staged package or vignette, which is a later snapshot than the release the article cites; they are listed because each rests on an exact formal example or derivation and its correction replaces a formula, a constant or the description of the set that is averaged, and each target says which premise is read from source code and lies outside what Lean can establish. The other nine confirmed errors are not targets because their corrections change no mathematical statement: P008-N017 (Moderate) is the horizontal placement of the band estimates in the bottom panel of Figure 8, established by recalculation from archived data (the band convention on which it rests is P008-T17 (b)); P008-E006 is an argument name; P008-E009 and P008-E012 concern the typesetting of the printed calls, an input guard of the later package and the wording of a numerical default; P008-N006 and P008-N007 concern the reproducibility of the toy intervals and of the smoothed curve with the staged copies of the package; P008-N005 is the colour key of Figure 3; P008-E010 is copy-editing (the mathematical content of the garbled sentence of p. 144 is in P008-T3, P008-T4 and P008-T22); P008-E011 is bibliographic. Findings classed as a clarity note (P008-E008), as not confirmed (P008-E001, P008-N003, P008-N013), as undetermined (P008-N008, P008-N010, P008-N011, P008-N014, P008-N015) or as out of scope (P008-E013, P008-E014) are outside the brief.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6, the permutation test of the cumulative effect between 1 and 2.5 km (the printed SpatialEffect() and SpatialEffectTest() calls, the two percentiles, and “thus significant with $p < 0.05$”), read as the sharp-null randomization test of the experiment: exact examples in which the law of unrestricted permutations is not the law of the design
canonical_claim.location: p. 153 (PDF p. 16); the design sentences on p. 151 (PDF p. 14), p. 145 (PDF p. 8) and p. 142 (PDF p. 5)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed passages] [p. 151] “The study was carried out in 121 villages, 60 of which were randomly assigned to treatment (Fig. 6).” [p. 145] “The permutation test can be adjusted to account for blocking or clustering in experimental design.” [p. 153, the two calls as printed; “/” marks a line break of the paper and the doubled apostrophes are the paper's] dVec = seq(from=0, to=20/111, by=5/111) AMRest <- Spatial / Effect(ras = ras, ras_Z = ras_Z, treatment = ''treatment'', / dVec = dVec, smooth= 1, cutoff = 10000, / dist.metric = ''Geodesic'') ... testResult <- SpatialEffectTest(AMRest, test.range = c(1/111, / 2.5/111)) [p. 153] “For the cumulative effect between 1 km and 2.5 km, the 0.025 and .975 percentiles of the sharp null permutation distribution are $-0.0304$ and $0.0336$ (that is, a 3.04 percentage point reduction to a 3.36 percentage point increase in the cumulative probability of forest loss), respectively. The estimated cumulative effect between 1 km and 2.5 km is $-0.0321$ (i.e., a 3.21 percentage point reduction). The cumulative effect between 1 km and 2.5 km is thus significant with $p < 0.05$. Beyond 2.5 km, spillover effects of the PES program appear to be negligible.”

[What the printed calls do; from the validator] The calls pass neither blockvar nor clustvar. With those defaults the staged implementations draw assignments uniformly from the assignments of the 121 villages that have the observed number treated, 60.

[The design of the experiment; from the source study's supplement, not from the article] “each of the 7 subcounties”; “In advance of each lottery, we divided the sample villages in the subcounty into two sets, balanced on covariates.” Treatment was assigned by seven subcounty lotteries, each choosing which of two covariate-balanced lists of that subcounty's villages is treated.

[Claim refuted] That the percentiles of the statistic over uniformly drawn assignments with the observed number treated are the percentiles of its sharp-null randomization distribution whatever restrictions the design placed on the assignment; equivalently, that the observed assignment and its number treated determine the reference law of the test.

Exact examples (the validator's; integer and rational arithmetic).
(A) [The observed assignment and its treated count do not determine the design law.] Let $N = 121$, $M = 60$, $\Omega_U = \{z \in \{0,1\}^{121} : \sum_i z_i = 60\}$ and let $Q_U$ be the uniform law on $\Omega_U$, so $|\Omega_U| = \binom{121}{60}$. Fix any $z^{\mathrm{obs}} \in \Omega_U$ and label the units so that $z^{\mathrm{obs}}_i = 1$ for $i \in \{1,\dots,5\} \cup \{11,\dots,65\}$ and $z^{\mathrm{obs}}_i = 0$ for $i \in \{6,\dots,10\} \cup \{66,\dots,121\}$. Let $\Omega_B = \{z \in \{0,1\}^{121} : \sum_{i=1}^{10} z_i = 5,\ \sum_{i=11}^{121} z_i = 55\}$ and let $Q_B$ be the uniform law on $\Omega_B$, so $|\Omega_B| = \binom{10}{5}\binom{111}{55}$. Then $\Omega_B \subsetneq \Omega_U$; $Q_U(z^{\mathrm{obs}}) > 0$ and $Q_B(z^{\mathrm{obs}}) > 0$; and the assignment $z'$ that agrees with $z^{\mathrm{obs}}$ except that $z'_6 = 1$ and $z'_{11} = 0$ has $\sum_i z'_i = 60$, $Q_U(z') > 0$ and $Q_B(z') = 0$. So $Q_U \ne Q_B$, although both laws treat 60 of 121 units with probability one and both give the observed assignment positive probability.
(B) [The two reference laws give different tail probabilities, in either direction.] Four nodes, two treated. Let $y = (y_1,\dots,y_4)$ be circle averages that are fixed under the sharp null and $T(z) = \tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^4 z_i y_i - \tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^4 (1 - z_i) y_i$ (the Hajek contrast with $N_1 = N_0 = 2$). Unrestricted support: $\Omega_U = \{1100, 1010, 1001, 0110, 0101, 0011\}$ with the uniform law $Q_U$. Blocked design that treats exactly one node in each of the pairs $\{1,2\}$ and $\{3,4\}$: $\Omega_B = \{1010, 1001, 0110, 0101\}$ with the uniform law $Q_B$. Observed assignment $z^{\mathrm{obs}} = 1010$. For a law $Q$ write $p_Q(z) = Q(\{w : |T(w)| \ge |T(z)|\})$.
(B1) $y = (0, 1, 0, 1)$: $T$ equals $0, -1, 0, 0, 1, 0$ at $1100, 1010, 1001, 0110, 0101, 0011$; $T(z^{\mathrm{obs}}) = -1$; $p_{Q_U}(z^{\mathrm{obs}}) = 2/6 = 1/3$ and $p_{Q_B}(z^{\mathrm{obs}}) = 2/4 = 1/2$.
(B2) $y = (0, 1/3, 2/3, 1)$: $T$ equals $-2/3, -1/3, 0, 0, 1/3, 2/3$ at $1100, 1010, 1001, 0110, 0101, 0011$; $T(z^{\mathrm{obs}}) = -1/3$; $p_{Q_U}(z^{\mathrm{obs}}) = 4/6 = 2/3$ and $p_{Q_B}(z^{\mathrm{obs}}) = 2/4 = 1/2$.
Hence the tail probability computed from unrestricted permutations can be smaller (B1) or larger (B2) than the tail probability under the law of the design.

canonical_claim.note: P008-N012 is rated an error, Major (verdict confirmed in part after the source study's supplement was read). The examples are the validator's (derivation.md, sections 3–5; design_checks.txt) and are the exact formal content on which the finding rests: they show that the reference law is not identified by the observed count and that the two laws give different tail probabilities. They are not a counterexample to the printed numbers: the validator states that the Uganda percentiles, statistic and p-value were not reconstructed, that no corrected p-value or its direction is established, and that a test under the documented design could still reject at 5%. The call as printed also has the misprinted step 5/111 (P008-T12, P008-T13) and typesetting defects; they are not used here. The design passage has no page image in the staged article and is transcribed from the settled record.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6, the claim “The cumulative effect between 1 km and 2.5 km is thus significant with $p < 0.05$”, corrected (formal content: when the percentiles of a permutation distribution give a valid sharp-null test)
canonical_claim.location: p. 153 (PDF p. 16); with p. 151 (PDF p. 14), p. 145 (PDF p. 8), p. 144 (PDF p. 7) and p. 142 (PDF p. 5)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected claim; Sol's smallest repair] “Qualify the unrestricted permutation result as a benchmark and withdraw the design-valid significance claim pending reanalysis. To reinstate that claim, regenerate the sharp-null distribution using the documented subcounty balanced-list lotteries, or a justified conditional law, and recompute the quantiles and p-value. Adding blockvar alone would not impose the covariate-balance restrictions.”

[Formal content]
(a) [A randomization test is valid when its reference law is the law of the design.] Let $\Omega$ be a finite set of assignments, $Q$ a probability distribution on $\Omega$ and $T : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$. For $z \in \Omega$ put $p_Q(z) = Q(\{w \in \Omega : |T(w)| \ge |T(z)|\})$. If $\mathbf{Z}$ has distribution $Q$, then $\Pr(p_Q(\mathbf{Z}) \le \delta) \le \delta$ for every $\delta \in [0,1]$. The same holds conditionally: if $A \subseteq \Omega$ has $Q(A) > 0$ and $Q_A = Q(\cdot \mid A)$, then $\Pr(p_{Q_A}(\mathbf{Z}) \le \delta \mid \mathbf{Z} \in A) \le \delta$. Under the sharp null $Y_x(\mathbf{z}) = Y_x(\mathbf{0})$ for all $x$ and $\mathbf{z}$, the circle averages $\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}; d)$ do not depend on the assignment, so the cumulative statistic $\sum_{d \in D}\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(d)$ is a fixed function $T$ of the assignment and (a) applies with $Q$ the law of $\mathbf{Z}$ under the design.
(b) [When the law of unrestricted permutations is that law.] If $Z_1,\dots,Z_N$ are independent with a common $\Pr(Z_i = 1) = p \in (0,1)$, then for every $M \in \{0,\dots,N\}$ and every $z \in \{0,1\}^N$ with $\sum_i z_i = M$, $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = z \mid \sum_i Z_i = M) = \binom{N}{M}^{-1}$. The same uniform law $Q_U$ on $\Omega_U = \{z : \sum_i z_i = M\}$ is the design law when exactly $M$ of the $N$ nodes are treated and all $\binom{N}{M}$ subsets are equally likely. For these designs the reference law used by the printed calls is the (conditional) design law and (a) applies to it.
(c) [When it is not.] If the law of the design, conditional on the number treated, is not $Q_U$ — for example if its support is a proper subset $\Omega_B \subsetneq \Omega_U$, as for a design with fixed numbers treated within blocks, and as for the documented design, in which the treated villages of each of the seven subcounties are one of two lists fixed before the lottery — then (a) gives level $\delta$ for the tail probability computed with the design's law and gives nothing for the tail probability computed with $Q_U$; the two differ in general, in either direction (P008-T1, (B1): $1/3$ against $1/2$; (B2): $2/3$ against $1/2$). Consequently the comparison of $-0.0321$ with the percentiles $-0.0304$ and $0.0336$ of the unrestricted permutation distribution does not establish $p < 0.05$ for the experiment; the percentiles have to be recomputed under the law of the seven subcounty lotteries or a justified conditional law of it.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Sections 2.3, 3 and 5: the rule that rejects the sharp null when the statistic lies outside the $\delta/2$ and $1-\delta/2$ percentiles of the null permutation distribution, as an error-rate-$\delta$ test (“approximately in exact finite samples”), and its use in the toy example with six assignments
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed rule and its use] [p. 144] “For a two-way test of the sharp null hypothesis for a specific AMR value with an error rate of $\delta$, one can evaluate the estimated AMR relative to the $\delta/2$ and $1 - \delta/2$ quantiles of the null permutation distribution. (We use $\delta$ for the inferential error rate here so as not to confuse with $\alpha$, which is defined above to characterize the experimental design.) Such tests of the sharp null are approximately in exact finite samples, where the quality of the approximation depends the extent to the which the simulated permutations cover the full set of possible permutations. We can also use a permutation test to test linear functionals of the AMR, such as the mean or cumulative AMR within a range of distance values. To do so, one evaluates the estimated AMR functional value against the null permutation distribution of the functional values.” [p. 146] “At each distance $d$, the sharp null hypothesis of no effect is rejected if the AMR estimate is smaller than the $\delta/2$ percentile or larger than the $1 - \delta/2$ percentile.” [p. 148, footnote 5] “The number doesn't make any difference here as there are in total 6 assignments.” [pp. 149–150] “The 0.025 and .975 percentiles of the sharp null permutation distribution of the cumulative effect are $-7.97$ and $7.97$, respectively, while the actual cumulative effect is 12.38. Based on an error rate of $\delta = 0.05$, we would reject the sharp null hypothesis that there is no cumulative effect on the distance interval of $[0.1, 0.5]$.”

[Claim refuted] That the rule “reject when the statistic is smaller than the $\delta/2$ percentile or larger than the $1-\delta/2$ percentile of the null permutation distribution”, with the percentiles computed as in the toy example (interpolated quantiles of the enumerated distribution, (S9)(i)), rejects a true sharp null with probability at most $\delta$ once all assignments are enumerated; in particular, that the toy example's decision is a rejection at error rate $\delta = 0.05$.

Counterexample (the validator's; exact arithmetic). Four intervention nodes at $x(i) = (10(i-1), 0)$, $i = 1,\dots,4$, in a rectangle $\mathcal{X}$ that contains the closed discs of radius 1 about them (the four discs are disjoint). Potential outcomes: $Y_x(\mathbf{z}) = i - 1$ if $\|x - x(i)\| \le 1$ for some $i$, and $Y_x(\mathbf{z}) = 0$ otherwise, for every assignment $\mathbf{z}$; so the sharp null $Y_x(\mathbf{z}) = Y_x(\mathbf{0})$ holds. Design: exactly two of the four nodes are treated, the six assignments $\Omega = \{1100, 1010, 1001, 0110, 0101, 0011\}$ having probability $1/6$ each (this is also the law of four independent Bernoulli(1/2) assignments given that two are treated). canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Sections 2.3, 3 and 5: the permutation test of the sharp null and the toy example's conclusion on $[0.1, 0.5]$, corrected (inclusive randomization tail probabilities; no rejection at $\delta = 0.05$ with six assignments)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected text; Sol's prior-correction text, confirmed by the validators] “With all six assignments enumerated, the observed cumulative statistic on [0.1,0.5], in the implemented sum units, is 8.00. Its inclusive two-sided randomization p-value is 2/6 = 0.33, so the sharp null is not rejected at delta = 0.05. Use inclusive randomization tail probabilities or conservatively calibrated discrete critical values; interpolated .025/.975 quantiles need not give a level-.05 test even with full enumeration.”

[Formal content]
(a) [Six assignments cannot give a 5% rejection.] Let $\Omega$ be the six assignments of four nodes with exactly two treated, each with probability $1/6$, and let $m_i(d)$, $i = 1,\dots,4$, be any real numbers (the circle averages, fixed under the sharp null). For $z \in \Omega$ put $T_d(z) = \tfrac12\sum_i z_i m_i(d) - \tfrac12\sum_i (1 - z_i) m_i(d)$ and, for distances $d_1,\dots,d_J$ and real weights $a_1,\dots,a_J$, $S(z) = \sum_{j=1}^J a_j T_{d_j}(z)$. Then $\mathbf{1} - z \in \Omega$, $\mathbf{1} - z \ne z$ and $S(\mathbf{1} - z) = -S(z)$ for every $z \in \Omega$. Consequently $p(z) := \#\{w \in \Omega : |S(w)| \ge |S(z)|\}/6 \ge 2/6 = 1/3$ for every $z \in \Omega$. Moreover every nonempty $R \subseteq \Omega$ has probability $|R|/6 \ge 1/6 > 1/20$, so a test of the sharp null whose rejection region is a set of assignments (given the fixed outcomes) has level $0.05$ on this support only if it never rejects.
(b) [The calibrated rule.] Let $\Omega$ be a finite set of assignments, $Q$ the law of the design on $\Omega$ and $S : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$. With $p(z) = Q(\{w \in \Omega : |S(w)| \ge |S(z)|\})$ (for uniform $Q$: $\#\{w : |S(w)| \ge |S(z)|\}/|\Omega|$, the observed assignment and all ties included) and $\mathbf{Z} \sim Q$, $\Pr(p(\mathbf{Z}) \le \delta) \le \delta$ for every $\delta \in [0,1]$. So with all assignments enumerated the test “reject when $p \le \delta$” has size at most $\delta$ exactly, possibly conservatively; enumeration does not give this property to the interpolated-percentile rule (P008-T3).
(c) [The toy example.] The statistic on $[0.1, 0.5]$ is the sum of the five AMR estimates at $d = 0.1, \dots, 0.5$; by the printed table it is $7.996$ up to rounding (P008-T11), not $12.38$. By (a) its inclusive two-sided randomization p-value is at least $1/3$, so the sharp null is not rejected at $\delta = 0.05$. (In the validators' reconstruction the six cumulative statistics are $\pm 7.99649$, $\pm 7.82109$, $\pm 4.44342$, the observed one is $7.99649$, and the p-value is exactly $2/6$.)
(d) [Sampled permutations.] If $\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{obs}}, \mathbf{Z}^{1}, \dots, \mathbf{Z}^{B}$ are independent draws from $Q$, then $p_B = \left(1 + \#\{b : |S(\mathbf{Z}^{b})| \ge |S(\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{obs}})|\}\right)/(B + 1)$ satisfies $\Pr(p_B \le \delta) \le \delta$ for every $\delta \in [0,1]$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3, the instruction on the spatial-HAC cutoff, with the toy example's choice “cutoff = .4”: an exact example in which a cutoff equal to the range of the effects omits half of the variance of the Hajek contrast
canonical_claim.location: p. 145 (PDF p. 8); toy cutoff on pp. 147–148 (PDF pp. 10–11) and the table on p. 149 (PDF p. 12)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed passages] [p. 145] “For the asymptotic variance estimator, users need to specify a distance threshold (cutoff) beyond which interference dependence does not exist. This can be based on substantive judgments about the likely spatial extent of interference, and can be varied as part of a sensitivity analysis.” [pp. 147–148] “The cutoff point for the spatial HAC variance is set to be 0.4 and the number of permutations is set to be 1000.” [p. 148, call] cutoff = .4, nPerms = 1000, smooth = 1) [p. 149] “The red dotted line is the 95% confidence interval based on the spatial-HAC standard errors.”

[Reading refuted] That a cutoff covering the distance over which an intervention changes outcomes (the reading on which the toy example's intervals, with a cutoff below every distance between nodes, are intervals that account for interference) makes the spatial-HAC variance account for the dependence between the node-level contributions to $\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(d)$.

Counterexample (the validator's; exact rational arithmetic). Two intervention nodes at $x(1) = (0,0)$ and $x(2) = (2,0)$; outcome points $(-1,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(3,0)$ with counting measure (the two nodes may be added to the field with the same outcome formula: they are at distance 0 or 2 from each node and do not enter a circle of radius 1). Potential outcomes $Y_x(\mathbf{z}) = \sum_{k=1}^{2} z_k \mathbf{1}\{\|x - x(k)\| \le 1\}$: additive, the same for both nodes, and zero beyond distance $r = 1$. Take $d = 1$. The circle about node 1 is $\{(-1,0), (1,0)\}$ and that about node 2 is $\{(1,0), (3,0)\}$, so $\mu_1(\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{z}); 1) = z_1 + \tfrac12 z_2$ and $\mu_2(\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{z}); 1) = z_2 + \tfrac12 z_1$. Design: $Z_1, Z_2$ independent Bernoulli(1/2). Then $\mu_i(1; 1, \alpha) = 5/4$, $\mu_i(0; 1, \alpha) = 1/4$ for $i = 1, 2$ and $\tau(1; \alpha) = 1$. With $m_1 = 5/4$, $m_0 = 1/4$ and the linearization contributions $\phi_i = 2Z_i(\mu_i - m_1) - 2(1 - Z_i)(\mu_i - m_0)$ of the Hajek contrast, the four assignments $(Z_1, Z_2) = (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)$ give $(\mu_1, \mu_2) = (0,0), (1/2, 1), (1, 1/2), (3/2, 3/2)$ and $\phi_1 = \phi_2 = 1/2, -1/2, -1/2, 1/2$; that is, $\phi_1 = \phi_2 = \tfrac12(2Z_1 - 1)(2Z_2 - 1)$. Hence $\mathrm{E}\phi_i = 0$, $\mathrm{Var}(\phi_1) = \mathrm{Var}(\phi_2) = 1/4$, $\mathrm{Cov}(\phi_1, \phi_2) = 1/4$, and
$\mathrm{Var}\left(\tfrac12(\phi_1 + \phi_2)\right) = 1/4$, whereas $\tfrac14\left(\mathrm{Var}(\phi_1) + \mathrm{Var}(\phi_2)\right) = 1/8$.
A cutoff $b = r = 1$ is smaller than the distance 2 between the two nodes, so the cutoff-$b$ sum of covariances $\tfrac14\sum_{i,j}\mathrm{Cov}(\phi_i, \phi_j)\mathbf{1}\{\|x(i) - x(j)\| \le b\}$ keeps only the diagonal and equals $1/8$: half of the variance.
Replication: for $M \ge 1$ take the pairs of nodes $(6g, 0), (6g + 2, 0)$ with outcome points $(6g - 1, 0), (6g + 1, 0), (6g + 3, 0)$, $g = 0, \dots, M - 1$, the same outcome rule, and $N = 2M$ independent Bernoulli(1/2) assignments. Then, with the same $m_1, m_0$, $\mathrm{Var}\left(N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\phi_i\right) = 1/(2N)$ while $N^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathrm{Var}(\phi_i) = 1/(4N)$, for every $M$; outcomes are bounded by 2, distinct nodes are at distance at least 2, and each circle average depends on at most two assignments.
[Asymptotic consequence drawn by the validator, not required of a formalization] $\sqrt{N}(\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(1) - 1)$ has limiting variance $1/2$ while $N$ times the diagonal-only (HC0) variance estimate converges to $1/4$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3, the instruction on the spatial-HAC cutoff, and the toy example's “Conley” intervals (cutoff 0.4), corrected: with cutoff 0.4 no pair of distinct nodes enters the variance estimator and the printed limits are HC0 limits
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected text; Sol's smallest repair] Keep the general guidance but make its object explicit: the cutoff must cover the dependence of the node-level estimating contributions at the radius being analyzed. For the toy example state: “With cutoff 0.4, no distinct pair of intervention nodes enters the variance estimator. These displayed limits equal HC0 limits and do not adjust for interference between nodes; they illustrate nominal intervals rather than calibrated inference in this four-node example.”

[Formal content]
(a) [A cutoff below the smallest distance between nodes gives HC0.] Let $D_{ij}$ be the distance between nodes $i$ and $j$ ($D_{ii} = 0$), let $N_1, N_0 \ge 1$, $M_i = \mu_i(\mathbf{Y}; d)$, $q_i = Z_i/N_1 - (1 - Z_i)/N_0$ and $e_i = M_i - \bar M_{Z_i}$, where $\bar M_1$ and $\bar M_0$ are the means of the $M_j$ over treated and over control nodes (so $\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(d) = \sum_i q_i M_i$ and the $e_i$ are the residuals of the regression of $M_i$ on an intercept and $Z_i$). The uniform-kernel spatial-HAC variance of the contrast with cutoff $c \ge 0$ is $\widehat{V}(c) = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N} q_i q_j e_i e_j \mathbf{1}\{D_{ij} \le c\}$; it is the $(2,2)$ entry of $(X'X)^{-1}\left[\sum_i\sum_j \mathbf{1}\{D_{ij} \le c\}\, e_i e_j X_i' X_j\right](X'X)^{-1}$ with rows $X_i = (1, Z_i)$, because $(0,1)(X'X)^{-1}X_i' = q_i$. If $D_{ij} > c$ for all $i \ne j$, then $\widehat{V}(c) = \sum_i q_i^2 e_i^2 = \sum_{i: Z_i = 1} e_i^2/N_1^2 + \sum_{i: Z_i = 0} e_i^2/N_0^2 = \widehat{V}(0)$, the heteroskedasticity-consistent (HC0) variance.
(b) [The toy example.] The four nodes of the toy example are at $x(1) = (2028297641/2147483648,\ 4318520789/2147483648)$, $x(2) = (7976664621/2147483648,\ 1029755657/268435456)$, $x(3) = (1053580245/536870912,\ 2017196647/2147483648)$, $x(4) = (7110225301/2147483648,\ 499145583/1073741824)$ (the validators' reconstruction from the staged vignette; the paper shows them only in Fig. 2). All six squared distances between distinct nodes exceed $(2/5)^2$; the smallest distance is $1.4295\ldots$. By (a), for these nodes $\widehat{V}(0.4) = \widehat{V}(0)$ at every distance $d$ and for every vector of circle averages, so the limits $\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(d) \mp z_{0.975}\sqrt{\widehat{V}(0.4)}$ computed with cutoff $0.4$ are the limits obtained with cutoff 0 (the validators reproduce the ten printed pairs Conley.CI.l, Conley.CI.u in this way to three decimals).
(c) [What the cutoff has to cover.] Suppose $\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{z}); d) = b_i + \sum_{k=1}^{N} a_{ik} z_k$ for real $b_i$, $a_{ik}$ and all $\mathbf{z} \in \{0,1\}^N$, and $Z_1,\dots,Z_N$ are independent Bernoulli(1/2). For any constants $m_1, m_0$ put $\phi_i = 2Z_i(\mu_i - m_1) - 2(1 - Z_i)(\mu_i - m_0)$, with $\mu_i = \mu_i(\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{Z}); d)$. Then $\mathrm{Cov}(\phi_i, \phi_j) = a_{ij} a_{ji}$ for all $i \ne j$. Hence $\mathrm{Var}\left(N^{-1}\sum_i \phi_i\right) = N^{-2}\left[\sum_i \mathrm{Var}(\phi_i) + \sum_{i \ne j} a_{ij} a_{ji}\right]$, and the sum restricted to pairs with $D_{ij} \le c$ equals it when $a_{ij} a_{ji} = 0$ for every pair with $D_{ij} > c$.
(d) [A sufficient geometric bound.] If node $k$ has no effect on points farther than $r$ from it, in the sense that $a_{ik}$ is an average over points $x$ with $d_i(x) = d$ of quantities that vanish when $\|x - x(k)\| > r$, then $a_{ik} = 0$ whenever $D_{ik} > d + r$ (triangle inequality), so a cutoff $c \ge d + r$ meets the condition of (c); a cutoff $c = r$ need not (P008-T5).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6, the parentheticals “(that is, a 3.04 percentage point reduction to a 3.36 percentage point increase in the cumulative probability of forest loss)” and “(i.e., a 3.21 percentage point reduction)”: an exact binary example in which the sum of the AMR estimates is $-0.0321$ and the change in the probability of loss is $-0.008025$
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed statement] “For the cumulative effect between 1 km and 2.5 km, the 0.025 and .975 percentiles of the sharp null permutation distribution are $-0.0304$ and $0.0336$ (that is, a 3.04 percentage point reduction to a 3.36 percentage point increase in the cumulative probability of forest loss), respectively. The estimated cumulative effect between 1 km and 2.5 km is $-0.0321$ (i.e., a 3.21 percentage point reduction). The cumulative effect between 1 km and 2.5 km is thus significant with $p < 0.05$. Beyond 2.5 km, spillover effects of the PES program appear to be negligible.”

[Claim refuted] That the unweighted sum of the AMR estimates (or of the AMRs) over the distances evaluated in a range is, after multiplication by 100, a change in percentage points of a probability of forest loss.

Counterexample (the validator's adjudicated construction; integer and rational arithmetic; a synthetic population, not Uganda data). Distances in kilometres.
1. $N = 4$ nodes with centres $c_0 = (0,0)$, $c_1 = (20,0)$, $c_2 = (0,20)$, $c_3 = (20,20)$. Radii $d_1, \dots, d_4 = 1, 3/2, 2, 5/2$. Let $M = 40000$ and, for $k = 1, \dots, M$, $\ell_k = 2k - M - 1$, $u_k = (M^2 - \ell_k^2)/(M^2 + \ell_k^2)$, $v_k = 2M\ell_k/(M^2 + \ell_k^2)$ and $x_{i,j,k} = c_i + d_j(u_k, v_k)$. The field is $\mathcal{X} = \{c_0, c_1, c_2, c_3\} \cup \{x_{i,j,k} : i = 0,\dots,3;\ j = 1,\dots,4;\ k = 1,\dots,M\}$, with Euclidean distance and counting measure.
2. $u_k^2 + v_k^2 = 1$, so $\|x_{i,j,k} - c_i\| = d_j$; the directions $(u_k, v_k)$ are distinct ($v_k/(1 + u_k) = \ell_k/M$ is strictly increasing in $k$); every point within $5/2$ of $c_i$ is at least $35/2$ from the other centres. Hence $|\mathcal{X}| = 640004$ and, for each $i$ and $j$, $\{x \in \mathcal{X} : \|x - c_i\| = d_j\} = \{x_{i,j,k} : k = 1,\dots,M\}$ has exactly $M$ points.
3. Design: $Z_0, \dots, Z_3$ independent Bernoulli(1/2). With $B = (B_0, B_1, B_2, B_3) = (400, 1000, 400, 1000)$, for every $\mathbf{z} \in \{0,1\}^4$: $Y_{c_i}(\mathbf{z}) = 0$ and $Y_{x_{i,j,k}}(\mathbf{z}) = \mathbf{1}\{k \le B_i - 321 z_i\}$. All potential outcomes are in $\{0, 1\}$ (1 = loss).
4. For every $i$, $j$ and $b \in \{0,1\}$: $\mu_i(b; d_j, \alpha) = (B_i - 321 b)/40000$, so $\tau_i(d_j; \alpha) = -321/40000$ and $\tau(d_j; \alpha) = -321/40000 = -0.008025$.
5. At the assignment $\mathbf{z}^* = (1,1,0,0)$ (probability $1/16$): $\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(d_j) = \frac{79 + 679}{2 \cdot 40000} - \frac{400 + 1000}{2 \cdot 40000} = -\frac{321}{40000}$ for each $j$, and the unweighted sum over the four radii is $\sum_{j=1}^{4}\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(d_j) = \sum_{j=1}^{4}\tau(d_j;\alpha) = -321/10000 = -0.0321$.
6. The probability of loss at a point drawn uniformly from the $640000$ circle points (equivalently: a uniformly drawn node, radius and circle point) is $Q_0 = (400 + 1000 + 400 + 1000)/160000 = 7/400$ when the point's own node is untreated and $Q_1 = (79 + 679 + 79 + 679)/160000 = 379/40000$ when it is treated; $Q_1 - Q_0 = -321/40000 = -0.008025$, i.e. $-0.8025$ percentage points, not $-3.21$. Every other normalized weighting of the four radii gives the same difference, because $\tau(d_j;\alpha)$ does not depend on $j$. Read as a change in this probability, the sum would give $Q_0 + (-321/10000) = -73/5000 < 0$.
7. Companion model on the same field: $Y_{c_i}(\mathbf{z}) = 0$ and $Y_{x_{i,j,k}}(\mathbf{z}) = 1 - z_i$. Then $\tau(d_j;\alpha) = -1$ for each $j$, the sum over the four radii is $-4$, and the sum of the Hajek estimates at $\mathbf{z}^*$ is $-4$. Since $a - b \ge -1$ for all $a, b \in [0,1]$, $-4$ is not the difference of two probabilities of any event.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6, the reported cumulative effect between 1 and 2.5 km and its two percentiles, corrected: values of the unscaled sum of the AMR estimates, with the normalization that makes a change in a probability
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected text; Sol's prior-correction text, confirmed by the validators] “For the unscaled sum of AMR estimates at the evaluated distances in the 1-2.5 km window, the 0.025 and 0.975 percentiles of the sharp-null permutation distribution are -0.0304 and 0.0336, respectively, and the observed sum is -0.0321. The observed sum lies below the lower reference quantile. Specify the actual grid and unit weights. These are values of the summed AMR functional. An equally weighted mean over the four radii indicated by Figure 8 would instead be approximately -0.0080, or a 0.8 percentage-point reduction for that explicitly normalized sampling target, with every permutation value divided by four as well.”

[Formal content]
(a) [Normalization.] Let all potential outcomes be in $\{0,1\}$ and put $q_b(d) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mu_i(b; d, \alpha)$ for $b \in \{0,1\}$. Then $0 \le q_b(d) \le 1$ and $\tau(d;\alpha) = q_1(d) - q_0(d)$. For radii $d_1,\dots,d_m$ and weights $w_j \ge 0$ with $\sum_j w_j = 1$ put $Q_b = \sum_{j=1}^{m} w_j q_b(d_j)$. Then $0 \le Q_b \le 1$, $Q_1 - Q_0 = \sum_{j=1}^{m} w_j \tau(d_j;\alpha)$, and so $\min_j \tau(d_j;\alpha) \le Q_1 - Q_0 \le \max_j \tau(d_j;\alpha)$ and $|Q_1 - Q_0| \le 1$. ($Q_b$ is the probability of loss at a point drawn by choosing a node uniformly, a radius $d_j$ with probability $w_j$ and a point from the normalized circle measure, the chosen node being set to $b$ and the other nodes assigned by the design.) With equal weights, $Q_1 - Q_0 = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\tau(d_j;\alpha)$.
(b) [The unweighted sum.] $S = \sum_{j=1}^{m}\tau(d_j;\alpha)$ is $m$ times the equal-weight difference of (a). If $\tau(d_j;\alpha) = t$ for all $j$, every normalized weighting gives $t$ and $S = mt$. $S$ need not lie in $[-1, 1]$ (P008-T7, item 7: $S = -4$), so it is not in general a difference of two probabilities.
(c) [Rescaling keeps the test.] For $m > 0$ and real numbers $S_{\mathrm{obs}}, S_1, \dots, S_B$: $S_b \le S_{\mathrm{obs}} \iff S_b/m \le S_{\mathrm{obs}}/m$; $|S_b| \ge |S_{\mathrm{obs}}| \iff |S_b/m| \ge |S_{\mathrm{obs}}/m|$; and every order statistic and every interpolated quantile $(1 - g)S_{(j)} + g S_{(j+1)}$ of $S_1/m, \dots, S_B/m$ is $1/m$ times that of $S_1, \dots, S_B$. With $m = 4$ the printed values become $-0.0304/4 = -19/2500 = -0.0076$, $-0.0321/4 = -321/40000 = -0.008025$ and $0.0336/4 = 21/2500 = 0.0084$, and $-0.008025 < -0.0076$ as $-0.0321 < -0.0304$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3, “a distance threshold (cutoff) beyond which interference dependence does not exist”, against the later archived package, in which the spatial-HAC threshold at the $j$-th distance of dVec is cutoff $+ j$: an exact example in which the variance of the same contrast at the same radius changes with the grid
canonical_claim.location: Article: p. 145 (PDF p. 8); toy call and table, pp. 148–149 (PDF pp. 11–12). Code, not in the article: staged package source, packages/SpatialEffect/YeWang1576-SpatialEffectPackage-7c873da/WangSamiiChangAronow_2024_replication/SpatialEffect/R/SpatialEffect.R, lines 199–229
canonical_claim.statement:
[Article, p. 145] “For the asymptotic variance estimator, users need to specify a distance threshold (cutoff) beyond which interference dependence does not exist. This can be based on substantive judgments about the likely spatial extent of interference, and can be varied as part of a sensitivity analysis.”

[Archived code as written; “/” marks a line break; the bracketed text summarizes omitted lines] c <- cutoff / for (d in 1:length(dVec)){ / dUp <- dVec[d] / [intervening lines: the regression of the circle averages at dUp on an intercept and treatment, with residuals res_d] / if (cutoff > 0){ / c <- cutoff + d / } / Conley_result <- ConleySE(as.vector(res_d), as.matrix(W_meat), as.matrix(dist), as.double(c), as.integer(k)) / VCE_d <- t(XX_mat_inv) %*% Conley_result[["VCE_meat"]] %*% XX_mat_inv / [with edf = FALSE] Conley.SE[d] <- sqrt(VCE_d[2, 2])
Here d is the position of the distance in dVec (1, 2, ...) and dUp is the distance itself; the threshold passed to the variance routine is cutoff + d, not cutoff.

[Statement refuted] That this code computes the spatial-HAC variance of the unsmoothed contrast at a radius with the user's distance threshold; equivalently, that its reported variance at a radius is a function of the circle averages at that radius, the treatment vector, the distances between nodes and the cutoff.

[Formal model of the computation; uniform kernel, no covariates, equal weights, edf = FALSE] At the $j$-th element of dVec: $X$ has rows $(1, Z_i)$; $\mu$ is the vector of circle averages at that radius; $\hat\beta = (X'X)^{-1}X'\mu$; $r = \mu - X\hat\beta$; $a = (0,1)(X'X)^{-1}X'$; $g_i = a_i r_i$; $K_{il}(c) = \mathbf{1}\{D_{il} \le c\}$ with $D$ the matrix of distances between nodes; the reported variance of the treatment coefficient is $V(c) = g'K(c)g$, with $c = \text{cutoff} + j$ when cutoff $> 0$.

Counterexample (the validator's; exact rational arithmetic). Four nodes at $(0,0), (2,0), (4,0), (6,0)$ with treatment indicators $(0, 0, 1, 1)$; the outcome field equals $0, 2, 4, 6$ on the closed discs of radius $3/10$ about the four nodes and $0$ elsewhere, so the circle averages are $\mu = (0, 2, 4, 6)$ at every radius in $\{1/10, 1/5, 3/10\}$; cutoff $= 2/5$. Then $\hat\beta = (1, 4)$, the contrast is $4$, $r = (-1, 1, -1, 1)$, $a = (-1/2, -1/2, 1/2, 1/2)$ and $g = (1/2, -1/2, -1/2, 1/2)$.
(i) Grid dVec $= (1/5, 3/10)$: the radius $1/5$ is at position 1, $c = 2/5 + 1 = 7/5 < 2$, $K$ is the identity and $V = \sum_i g_i^2 = 1$.
(ii) Grid dVec $= (1/10, 1/5, 3/10)$: the radius $1/5$ is at position 2, $c = 2/5 + 2 = 12/5$, $K_{il} = 1$ exactly when $|i - l| \le 1$, and $V = 1 + 2(g_1 g_2 + g_2 g_3 + g_3 g_4) = 1 + 2(-\tfrac14 + \tfrac14 - \tfrac14) = 1/2$.
The same contrast, at the same radius, with the same data and cutoff, is given variance $1$ or $1/2$ according to whether the unrelated radius $1/10$ is in the grid.
(iii) [Incompatibility with the printed toy table.] In the toy example the four nodes lie in $[0,4]^2$, so every squared distance between nodes is at most $32$. At $d = 0.6$, the sixth element of dVec $= 0.1, 0.2, \dots, 2$, the code's threshold is $c = 0.4 + 6 = 32/5$ and $(32/5)^2 = 1024/25 > 32$, so $K_{il} = 1$ for all $i, l$ and $V = \left(\sum_i g_i\right)^2 = \left((0,1)(X'X)^{-1}X'r\right)^2 = 0$ for every vector of circle averages and every assignment with both arms present, since $X'r = 0$. The interval would have width zero; the printed row for $d = 0.6$ is $1.700$, $-0.038$, $3.438$, of width $3.476$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The spatial-HAC threshold of the unsmoothed estimator in the archived package, corrected to the user's cutoff at every distance (Section 3, “a distance threshold (cutoff)”)
canonical_claim.location: Article: p. 145 (PDF p. 8). Code, not in the article: staged package source, packages/SpatialEffect/YeWang1576-SpatialEffectPackage-7c873da/WangSamiiChangAronow_2024_replication/SpatialEffect/R/SpatialEffect.R, lines 199–229 (line 216: c <- cutoff + d)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Correction; Sol's smallest repair] “Under the documented convention that cutoff is the final node-pair dependence bandwidth, delete the positive-cutoff reassignment c <- cutoff + d and retain c <- cutoff.” (If cutoff is meant as an underlying interference range that has to be enlarged for circle averages, the enlargement must be an explicitly justified function of the distance dUp, in the units of the distance matrix; no rule may use the position in the grid.)

[Formal content] Notation as in P008-T9: $X$ with rows $(1, Z_i)$ and both arms present, $\mu$ the circle averages at the radius, $r = \mu - X(X'X)^{-1}X'\mu$, $a = (0,1)(X'X)^{-1}X'$, $g_i = a_i r_i$, $K_{il}(c) = \mathbf{1}\{D_{il} \le c\}$, $V(c) = g'K(c)g$.
(a) [Corrected rule.] With $c = \text{cutoff}$ at every element of dVec, the variance reported at a radius is $V(\text{cutoff}) = g'K(\text{cutoff})g$, a function of $(\mu, \mathbf{Z}, D, \text{cutoff})$ only; it is therefore the same for every grid dVec that contains the radius. In the example of P008-T9 it is $1$ on both grids ($\text{cutoff} = 2/5 < 2$, $K$ the identity, $V = \sum_i g_i^2 = 1$).
(b) [Identity used in P008-T9 (iii).] If $K_{il} = 1$ for all $i, l$, then $g'Kg = \left(\sum_i a_i r_i\right)^2 = 0$, because $\sum_i a_i r_i = (0,1)(X'X)^{-1}X'r$ and $X'r = 0$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 5, toy example: “the actual cumulative effect is 12.38” on the interval $[0.1, 0.5]$, corrected to 8.00
canonical_claim.location: p. 149 (PDF p. 12), last two lines; table on the same page
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] “To further test this initial inference regarding effects at small values of $d$, we use SpatialEffectTest() to examine whether the cumulative effect is statistically significant on the interval $[0.1, 0.5]$: testResult <- SpatialEffectTest(AMRest, c(0.1, 0.5)) The 0.025 and .975 percentiles of the sharp null permutation distribution of the cumulative effect are $-7.97$ and $7.97$, respectively, while the actual cumulative effect is 12.38.” Printed table, columns dVec and AMR_est: $(0.1, 1.491)$, $(0.2, 1.550)$, $(0.3, 1.550)$, $(0.4, 1.691)$, $(0.5, 1.714)$, $(0.6, 1.700)$, $(0.7, 1.678)$, $(0.8, 1.002)$, $(0.9, -0.816)$, $(1.0, -0.791)$.

[Corrected] “... while the actual cumulative effect is 8.00” (unrounded in the validator's reconstruction: $7.99649$); the interval $[0.1, 0.5]$ and the percentiles $-7.97$ and $7.97$ are kept.

[Formal content] The cumulative effect is the sum of the AMR estimates at the distances of dVec in the range (S7).
(a) $1.491 + 1.550 + 1.550 + 1.691 + 1.714 = 7.996 = 1999/250$.
(b) If real numbers $a, b, c, e, f$ satisfy $|a - 1.491| \le 1/2000$, $|b - 1.550| \le 1/2000$, $|c - 1.550| \le 1/2000$, $|e - 1.691| \le 1/2000$ and $|f - 1.714| \le 1/2000$ (every rounding of the estimates to three decimals), then $7.9935 \le a + b + c + e + f \le 7.9985$; in particular $|(a + b + c + e + f) - 12.38| > 1/200$, so the sum cannot be printed as $12.38$, and $a + b + c + e + f > 7.975$, so it still exceeds every number printed as $7.97$.
(c) The sum through $d = 0.8$ is $7.996 + 1.700 + 1.678 + 1.002 = 12.376 = 1547/125$, which is printed as $12.38$ to two decimals.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6, the distance grid as printed (“with a step size of $5/111 \approx 0.045$”; by=5/111) with the test range c(1/111, 2.5/111): no grid point lies in the range
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] “Since 1 decimal degree is approximately 111 km, the distance values we select are between 0 and $20/111 \approx 0.18$, with a step size of $5/111 \approx 0.045$.” [Calls as printed; “/” marks a line break of the paper] dVec = seq(from=0, to=20/111, by=5/111) AMRest <- Spatial / Effect(ras = ras, ras_Z = ras_Z, treatment = ''treatment'', / dVec = dVec, smooth= 1, cutoff = 10000, / dist.metric = ''Geodesic'') ... testResult <- SpatialEffectTest(AMRest, test.range = c(1/111, / 2.5/111)) [Reported] the 0.025 and .975 percentiles $-0.0304$ and $0.0336$ and the estimated cumulative effect $-0.0321$ “between 1 km and 2.5 km”.

[Refutation; exact arithmetic] The printed grid is $d_k = 5k/111$, $k = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ (that is $0, 5, 10, 15, 20$ km at 111 km per degree); the next value $25/111$ exceeds $20/111$. The test range is $[1/111, 5/222]$. $d_k$ lies in it if and only if $1 \le 5k \le 5/2$, which holds for no integer $k$ ($5 \cdot 0 = 0 < 1$ and $5k \ge 5 > 5/2$ for $k \ge 1$). So the set of evaluated distances in the range is empty and, for any real values of the AMR estimates on the grid, the statistic “sum of the AMR estimates within the specified range” is the empty sum $0$, for the observed assignment and for every permuted assignment; every quantile of its permutation distribution is $0$. The reported $-0.0321$, $-0.0304$ and $0.0336$ are nonzero, so they are not the outputs of the printed commands on the printed grid.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The test statistic of SpatialEffectTest(): “the null permutation distribution of the sum of the AMR estimates within the specified range” (p. 146; (S7)). R's seq(from, to, by) returns from, from + by, ... up to the largest value not exceeding to. The range is closed (the staged implementation selects distances $\ge$ test.range[1] and $\le$ test.range[2]).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 2.2, the display defining the average marginalized response $\tau(d;\alpha)$, corrected (the equality sign restored, the bars removed, the index set written out)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] “Working with these terms, our target quantity is the average marginalized response (AMR) for distance $d$, which is simply the average $d$-radius effect over the intervention nodes: $\tau(d;\alpha) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tau_i(d;\alpha)\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[\bar{\mu}_i(1; d, \alpha) - \bar{\mu}_i(0; d, \alpha)\right].$ The interpretation of the AMR for distance $d$ is the average effect of switching a node $i \in \mathcal{N}$ to treatment on points at distance $d$ from that node, marginalized over possible realizations of treatment statuses in other intervention nodes.”

[Corrected; Sol's smallest repair] $\tau(d;\alpha) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tau_i(d;\alpha) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[\mu_i(1; d, \alpha) - \mu_i(0; d, \alpha)\right]$, with $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ in place of $i \in \mathcal{N}$ (or $\mathcal{N} = \{1,\dots,N\}$ defined).

[Formal content] (a) With $\tau_i(d;\alpha) = \mu_i(1; d, \alpha) - \mu_i(0; d, \alpha)$ (p. 143), $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tau_i(d;\alpha) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[\mu_i(1; d, \alpha) - \mu_i(0; d, \alpha)\right]$. (b) The printed display, read literally (juxtaposition as a product, $\bar{\mu}_i = \mu_i$), gives $A \cdot A$ with $A = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \tau_i(d;\alpha)$, which equals $A$ only when $A \in \{0, 1\}$; for example $N = 2$, $(\mu_1(1), \mu_2(1)) = (3, 7)$, $(\mu_1(0), \mu_2(0)) = (0, 2)$ gives $A = 4$ and $A \cdot A = 16$.
